articleSummary: Early summer in China sees peak tick activity (April–October), with grass ticks lurking in grass and woods. Ticks are small before feeding but enlarge after biting; they don’t fly or jump and can transmit diseases such as severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), Lyme disease, and tick-borne encephalitis. The bite is often painless due to anesthetic saliva. Do not slap, pull, or burn; remove with a narrow-tipped tweezers, gripping the head and pulling straight up without twisting. Disinfect the wound and save the tick in a sealed container for lab ID; seek hospital if mouthparts remain embedded. Monitor for two weeks; seek care if fever, rash (bull's-eye around bite or widespread red spots), altered mental state, headache, myalgia, or cellulitis. Prevention: wear light clothing, tuck cuffs, avoid sandals; use DEET (≤30% for ages 2+ months) or picaridin (≤20% for 6+ months); bathe after returning; check skin and treat pets for ticks.

articleSummary: Dengue transmission in Brazil persists despite Wolbachia-infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, nicknamed 'wolbitos,' which block transmission. These four are linked to Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS). The fifth, Sin Nombre virus (SNV), is reported in the United States and Canada; Bayou virus (BAYV) in the United States (Louisiana, Texas); Black Creek Canal virus (BCCV) in Florida. Andes virus (ANDV) is from South America (Argentina, Chile) and has appeared in cruise-ship cases. ANDV is notable for human-to-human transmission, with sustained transmission a key surveillance concern. Variants five through eight are associated with hantavirus pulmonary syndromes: Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS) and Hantavirus Cardio-Pulmonary Syndrome (HCPS). As of 2026-05-12.

articleHeadline: Different strains of hantavirus attack different organs
articleSummary: Following reports linked to the cruise ship MV Hondius, as of 2026-05-12 hantaviruses—rodent-borne viruses—cause organ-specific disease whose pattern depends on the strain. Transmission occurs via rodent excreta and nesting material that can aerosolize; humans are typically infected by inhaling contaminated dust. In Europe and Asia, causes haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS); fatality up to 15% with Hantaan virus, while Puumala virus in Europe causes milder illness with fatalities under 1%. In India, infections mainly affect the lungs, with a case fatality rate estimated between 1% and 15% and overall outbreak risk deemed very low. In the Americas, hantaviruses generate hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, with fatalities above 35%. Andes virus (Argentina/Chile) can transmit person-to-person and causes severe lung disease with 35–50% fatality. Australia remains hantavirus-free.

articleHeadline: 초음파 쏘자 코로나19 바이러스 붕괴...새 감염 차단 가능성
articleSummary: Brazilian researchers at the University of São Paulo used ultrasound to disrupt the envelopes of SARS-CoV-2 and Influenza A (H1N1), markedly reducing infectivity. Exposing the viruses to 3–20 MHz ultrasound damaged the viral envelope, diminishing host-cell infection. In cell assays, SARS-CoV-2 spike protein and RNA signals were reduced or disappeared after treatment. The mechanism is acoustic resonance: when ultrasound matches the envelope’s natural vibration, energy concentrates and disrupts the envelope. Enveloped viruses may absorb energy more efficiently due to spherical geometry, while surrounding cells remain largely unharmed. This approach targets the virus’s physical structure rather than molecular pathways, potentially applicable across variants such as Delta and Omicron, and to other viruses; researchers are also exploring Dengue and Zika. However, further refinement and human trials are needed before clinical use.

articleSummary: Hantavirus consists of multiple viruses with two main disease-causing subtypes: a Western/Americas-type linked to Central and North America (and parts of Europe and the Mediterranean) and a Southeast Asia/East Asia-type. The Western type can cause severe pneumonia, cardiac and sometimes renal involvement; the Southeast Asia/East Asia type usually presents with influenza-like illness and can lead to hemorrhagic fever, gastrointestinal bleeding, nausea and vomiting. Hantavirus is zoonotic, transmitted from rodents (mice and guinea pigs) to humans; human-to-human transmission is rare except in very close, prolonged contact. Incubation is 1–8 weeks; early symptoms include headache, fever, myalgia, and nausea, with severe cases risking respiratory or renal failure and bleeding. Fatality rates are 15–40% for the Western/Americas-type and 10–12% for the East Asia type. No specific antiviral or vaccine; treatment is supportive. Prevention focuses on handwashing, masking in warehouses, and eliminating rodent habitats. Iran reports no current cases.

articleSummary: Hantavirus, spread mainly by rodents, causes Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS) and Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS). Human-to-human transmission is uncommon; infection occurs via inhalation of aerosolized rodent urine, droppings, or saliva, direct contact with contaminated material, or rarely rodent bites. As of May 12, 2026, cases have been reported worldwide, with notable activity in the Americas (USA, Canada, Argentina, Chile, Brazil) and a May 2026 South American ship- voyage-linked case. In Asia, China and South Korea report annual cases; Europe sees Puumala-type hantavirus circulating in Russia, Germany, and Scandinavian nations; India remains low but emphasizes precautions in rodent-dense areas. Symptoms emerge 1–8 weeks post-exposure: fever, headache, myalgia, fatigue; severe illness can include respiratory distress, cough, pneumonia, and kidney dysfunction. No vaccine or specific treatment exists; prevention focuses on rodent control, damp cleaning of contaminated areas with disinfectant, sealing food, and masks in rodent-affected zones.

articleSummary: Hantavirus in Taiwan is highlighted as a rodent-borne threat. Taiwan hosts eight hantavirus rodent reservoirs, including sewer rats and Asian house rats, with other listed hosts such as house shrews and red-backed species. articleHeadline: Expert Explains | Hantavirus is a warning: Why outbreaks like this may become more common
articleSummary: Hantavirus outbreaks highlight a rising pattern of zoonotic spillovers driven by deforestation, urban expansion, and industrial farming. As forests are cleared and agriculture intensifies, wildlife reservoirs increasingly intersect with people, while climate change shifts vectors and animal movements, boosting spillover risk. Spillovers appear driven by conditions that bring pathogens into contact with humans and compress containment windows by travel and trade. The two main threat pathways are industrial livestock farming—creating dense, genetically similar animal populations that can amplify pathogens such as influenza—and habitat fragmentation from deforestation—pushing bats and rodents into human-modified areas, as seen with Nipah and Ebola. Surveillance remains underfunded and reactive; veterinary and wildlife monitoring lag behind clinical reporting, though One Health efforts exist in places like India. Climate-driven shifts in vector ranges (Aedes, ticks, Anopheles) and altered animal behavior create new contact points, underscoring the need for early detection.

articleSummary: Cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae, remains a seventh-pandemic, waterborne infection transmitted by the faecal-oral route, with endemic foci in South Asia, notably the Ganges delta region of India and Bangladesh. articleSummary: Hantavirus is a rodent-borne virus causing two deadly diseases: HPS and HFRS. articleSummary: Andes virus hantavirus has drawn global attention after passengers aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship were affected, with three deaths. Indonesia’s BRIN notes hantavirus spreads mainly via rodents—Rattus rattus, R. norvegicus, field mice, and wild mice in homes, farms, and forests. Its reservoir, the Andes virus, is the wild rodent Oligoryzomys longicaudatus found in Patagonia, Argentina and Chile; humans become infected by inhaling particles from rodent urine, feces, or saliva. Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome can cause severe pneumonia and respiratory failure; early symptoms mimic influenza—fever, myalgia, headache, nausea, malaise, GI upset—leading to diagnostic delays. From 2024 through week 16 of 2026, Indonesia reports 23 hantavirus cases and 3 deaths; 251 suspected cases (225 negative, 3 not tested). Geographically, Jakarta and Yogyakarta each report six cases, with additional cases in West Java and other provinces.
notes: 記事は Andes virus ハンタウイルスの国際的な cruise ship での集団発生（3名死亡）と、インドネシアにおける継続的な地域流行（2024〜2026年第16週で23確認例・3死亡、251疑い例）を報告。ジャカルタとヨグヤカルタ各6例、西ジャワでも追加報告あり。Bluedot APIは Arizona/Chile/Argentina も発生地域として列挙しているが、記事サマリーの主題はインドネシアの流行。cruise ship は国際拡散のリスク要因。

articleSummary: Indonesia reports 23 laboratory-confirmed hantavirus cases over the past three years, with 3 deaths; current evidence shows no human-to-human transmission. All confirmed cases involve the Seoul virus, carried primarily by the brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), not Andes virus. The largest annual surge occurred in 2025 with 17 cases; 2024 had 1 case; 2026 has 5 cases to date. Transmission occurs through inhalation of aerosolized excreta (urine, feces, or saliva) from infected rats, not rat bites. The virus has been detected in nine provinces, with Jakarta and DI Yogyakarta at the forefront of the outbreak. Rodent carriers have been found across 29 provinces, underscoring widespread public-health risk. Hantavirus can cause HFRS (hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome) or HPS (hantavirus pulmonary syndrome); to date, no HPS cases have been reported in Indonesia.

articleSummary: As of 12 May 2026, hantavirus transmission differs from Covid-19: it requires a rodent intermediary, with infection risk from contact with urine, feces, or saliva of infected rats, especially in dirty environments after floods. Indonesia’s Deputy Health Minister Dante Saksono Harbuwono notes rats as reservoirs, with household rats and post-flood conditions elevating risk. The pattern resembles leptospirosis, prompting a new Kemenkes protocol: any suspected leptospirosis patient should be tested for hantavirus. The key difference is that hantavirus is viral, not bacterial like leptospirosis. There is currently no strong evidence of human-to-human transmission for HFRS or HPS. Three deaths aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius are under investigation to determine possible hantavirus human-to-human spread. The Hondius variant has not been detected in Indonesia. Public advisories urge environmental cleanliness and rodent control; Indonesian authorities reiterate vigilance in Bandung and other flood-prone areas.

articleSummary: Hantavirus infections are again being reported in several countries, with the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warning against vacuuming or dry sweeping rodent droppings to prevent airborne transmission. Transmission occurs chiefly via inhalation of aerosolized particles from rodent urine, droppings, or nesting material, risking Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS), which has about a one‑third fatality rate. For cleanup, wear rubber or plastic gloves; ventilate the area by opening doors/windows for at least 30 minutes; apply a disinfectant or household bleach solution (1.5 cups bleach to 4 liters water) to saturate the area and leave at least five minutes; then wipe with paper towels and dispose in a covered trash bin, regularly emptied. After cleaning, use wet methods to minimize aerosol generation and protect the respiratory system. The report cites Times of India as a source; no laboratory confirmation details or data on imported/exported cases are included.

articleHeadline: How dangerous is hantavirus pulmonary syndrome? Prevention tips explained
articleSummary: Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome is a serious lung disease transmitted by rodents via saliva, droppings and urine that can be inhaled. Store grains, animal feed and foods in sturdy metal or thick plastic containers with secure lids to limit contamination. Early symptoms include fever and fatigue and muscle pain with shivering, which can progress to breathing difficulties; seek urgent care if breathing symptoms arise after exposure. Prevention is hygiene and caution.

articleHeadline: What Are Indonesia's Guidelines for Hantavirus Prevention?
articleSummary: Indonesia's Health Ministry published hantavirus prevention guidelines in May 2023, describing the disease as an 'iceberg phenomenon' due to limited diagnostics and underreporting. Globally, about 200,000 cases occur annually with 1–50% fatality; infections have been reported in China, South Korea, Japan, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, and Indonesia. Indonesia first documented human Orthohantavirus in 1991 at Maumere Port, Flores, with 13 of 100 tested positive. Guidelines call for strengthened surveillance, clinical management, specimen governance, risk-factor control, risk communication, and community empowerment amid diagnostic limits. Diagnostics rely on serological ELISA and RT-PCR; infection prevention requires PPE and proper waste management. Environmental controls target rats/shrews via sanitation, sealed entry points, traps, rodenticides, and reservoir monitoring, focusing on port workers, farmers, and sanitation-poor communities. As of 11 May 2026, no HPS cases; suspected cases are HFRS; a close-contact from MV Hondius tested negative.

articleSummary: On 2026-05-12, Mato Grosso do Sul’s State Health Secretariat reports a suspected hantavirus case in Campo Grande under investigation with up to 60 days to conclude. No confirmed hantavirus case in MS since 2019; over 11 years the state has 107 suspected cases and 7 confirmed. Hantavirus disease is mainly transmitted by inhalation of particles from urine, feces, or saliva of wild rodents; marsupials and bats are less common. The Centro-Oeste, Sul and Sudeste regions have the highest confirmed case percentages, with most transmission in rural, agricultural settings. Early symptoms are non-specific—fever, myalgias, back and abdominal pain, fatigue, headache, and GI symptoms—and may progress to dry cough, cardiopulmonary involvement, pulmonary edema, hypotension, and kidney impairment. Diagnosis relies on serology in reference labs; surveillance proceeds via SINAN to municipal epidemiology and SES zoonoses until closure. There are no specific antivirals; treatment is supportive and may require ICU. Prevention emphasizes reducing rodent habitats, secure food storage, and damp cleaning with PPE. Brazil reports no human-to-human transmission in 2026; Andes genotype not circulating.

There are over 20 hantavirus types; only some infect humans, with most variants found in Latin America (Argentina, Chile, Brazil); infections in Asia and Europe are rarer. Hantaviruses primarily circulate among rodents; human transmission is rare and usually via objects, dust, or food contaminated with rodent urine, feces, or saliva, with higher risk from prolonged exposure to contaminated environments or close contact with rodents. Symptoms include fever, headache, weakness, nausea, vomiting, muscle and abdominal pain; severe cases may lead to kidney failure and cardiovascular/respiratory complications. articleSummary: Twenty-three hantavirus infections have been detected in Indonesia to date, all of the Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) form and considered mild. Deputy Health Minister Dante says Indonesia distinguishes two hantavirus types: HFRS (roughly 15% fatality) and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS) (60–80% fatality). No human-to-human transmission has been proven, and current cases are not expected to trigger a global pandemic. Most infections arise after floods and involve rat reservoirs (house rats) with exposure to urine. Indonesia’s health authorities screen hantavirus in patients suspected of leptospirosis to bolster early detection. All confirmed cases in Indonesia so far are HFRS, with no severe HPS cases reported. Locations referenced include Indonesia and Bandung, West Java, with observations tied to post-flood scenarios and rodent exposure.

articleSummary: 11 hantavirus cases have been confirmed by the WHO, highlighting uncertainty about asymptomatic transmission of the Andes virus. If asymptomatic individuals can transmit, containment becomes harder because contact tracing and quarantine must account for the long incubation period and potential spread by non-symptomatic cases. On the Hondius voyage, inadequate tracing and quarantining may have allowed further infections among passengers. Diagnostics for Andes virus are limited: most available tests are RUO (Research Use Only) and largely sourced from China, not clinically approved, challenging regional labs. Experts urge active surveillance with highly sensitive molecular tests to detect presymptomatic infections, since viral shedding can begin soon after infection. A Zurich patient’s viral sequence is ~99% identical to the 2018 Argentina strain, suggesting genetic stability and supporting potential cross-utility of Argentine RUO kits.

articleSummary: Hantavirus is not yet an emergency as of May 12, 2026, despite the Hondius ship outbreak. Vaccines remain limited and strain-specific; Hantavax, authorized in South Korea and China since 1990, shows poor efficacy, protecting only two Asian hantavirus strains. A broadly protective solution would require multiple vaccines and costly, extensive testing across strains. RNA-based vaccines offer advantages: faster production and stronger immune responses than protein vaccines. Moderna, in collaboration with Korea University in Seoul since September 2024, is developing an RNA hantavirus vaccine, but animal testing has been completed while human trials lack funding. The WHO has identified a 100-day vaccine development goal. Korea accounts for about half of Asia’s hantavirus infections (roughly 400–500 per year, mainly among military). An Andes strain would not be covered by Asian vaccines. Monoclonal antibodies are being explored but remain preclinical.

articleSummary: During a hantavirus outbreak on MV Hondius, three deaths occurred and 11 passengers tested positive. By May 12, 125 passengers and crew had been evacuated to their countries of origin, per the WHO; two more tested positive after disembarking. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, said the risk of new infections is low. Hantaviruses are rodent-borne viruses; humans usually contract them by inhaling dust contaminated with rodent urine, saliva, or feces. In South America, hantavirus can cause Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS), which can affect the heart and lungs and be fatal. In Brazil, two cases were confirmed: Rio Grande do Sul (one death) and Minas Gerais (one death); neither linked to the cruise. Andes virus is the main transmitter in the Americas; human-to-human transmission is rare and requires close, prolonged contact. Incubation is 3–60 days; initial symptoms are nonspecific, then fever above 38°C, dyspnea, and dry cough; no vaccine; supportive care.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Hantavirus: a zoonotic emergency and the challenges of Infectiology.

articleSummary: Hantavirus infection exemplifies a zoonotic emergency, with spillover from rodent reservoirs to humans via inhalation of aerosols from urine, saliva, or dried feces. Clinically, Eurasian strains cause Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome; American strains cause Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome, both with abrupt vascular permeability, hypotension, edema, and risk of shock or ARDS. WHO notes the global spread risk remains low due to limited human-to-human transmission. Infectious disease specialists lead diagnostic and supportive care, with risk communication pivotal.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Understand Why the Hantavirus Is So Deadly and Where the Risk Is Greatest in Brazil.
articleHeadline: Entenda por que o hantavírus é tão letal e onde há mais risco no Brasil
articleSummary: Hantavirus infection in Brazil remains a public health concern due to high case fatality and its persistence in rural areas. Although rare, the disease can progress quickly from initial flu-like symptoms to hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, with severe dyspnea, hypotension, tachycardia, and acute respiratory failure. Transmission occurs mainly by inhaling dust contaminated with rodent urine, feces, or saliva. The highest risk areas are the South, rural parts of Southeast Brazil (São Paulo and Minas Gerais), and the Central-West in agricultural Mato Grosso and Goiás. Most infections affect rural male workers. Early diagnosis is challenging, and delays increase complications; rapid hospitalization reduces death risk. There is no specific antiviral treatment; prevention is key, including avoiding contact with wild rodents, moistening closed spaces before cleaning, wearing masks and gloves in risk areas, proper food storage, and reducing clutter and garbage.

articleHeadlineTranslated: 5 Diseases Transmitted by Rats Besides Hantavirus
articleHeadline: 5 Penyakit yang Ditularkan Tikus Selain Hantavirus
articleSummary: Five rat-borne diseases besides hantavirus are leptospirosis, salmonellosis, plague, rat-bite fever, and lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV). The Jakarta-based report cites transmission via rat urine, feces, saliva, bites, and contaminated food, with leptospirosis risk higher during rains or floods in areas with poor sanitation. Leptospirosis presents with fever, muscle pain, headache, and jaundice, potentially causing kidney or liver injury if untreated. Salmonellosis causes diarrhea, vomiting, fever, and abdominal cramps from contaminated food or surfaces; keeping food covered and kitchens clean reduces risk. Plague, caused by Yersinia pestis carried by fleas from rodents, can produce buboes, high fever, and flu-like symptoms; CDC notes about seven US cases per year. Rat-bite fever follows bites or scratches with fever, vomiting, muscle pain, and rash, sometimes affecting heart, brain, or lungs. LCMV can cause flu-like illness and, rarely, meningitis or encephalitis, with higher fetal risk.
